design_detail: Case series of 9 patients with lower urinary tract symptoms and chronic recreational ketamine use, from the Departments of Surgery and Pathology, St. Michael's Hospital and University of Toronto (Urology 2007;69:810–812; read as the published PDF, printed pp. 810–812). Every patient had a history and physical examination, cystoscopy, urine culture, urinalysis and urine cytology; 4 had bladder biopsies, all read by one pathologist; computed tomography and other tests were done 'as indicated', without saying in how many (p. 810). Three patients are described one by one (the index case, a 28-year-old man; a 25-year-old woman; a 17-year-old boy); the other 6 share one paragraph (p. 811). The course after stopping ketamine, with or without pentosan polysulfate, is described in words, without symptom scores, bladder measurements, repeat cystoscopy or a follow-up period. The Comment adds the analysis of one police-seized ketamine sample, not the patients' own (pp. 811–812). No comparison group. Submitted June 2006 (p. 810).
can_establish: That 9 people with chronic recreational ketamine use seen by one Toronto hospital service had irritative lower urinary tract symptoms with sterile urine cultures (and, in the index case, negative cytology), an inflamed and ulcerated bladder at cystoscopy and, in the 4 biopsied, denuded urothelium with granulation tissue, fibrosis and eosinophils, and that the authors saw symptoms ease after ketamine was stopped in some of them: the first published description of what the authors named ketamine-associated ulcerative cystitis, and a signal for later studies.
cannot_establish: That ketamine caused the cystitis (no comparison group, no testing for ketamine or other drugs, no amounts or duration of use, other causes not excluded patient by patient); how often bladder damage occurs in people who use ketamine (no denominator); what amount, frequency, duration or route carries risk (none reported); whether stopping ketamine or taking pentosan polysulfate helps, or how far symptoms recover (no measured outcome, no follow-up period, and the two were given together in 6 patients); or the long-term course, which the authors say remains to be defined (p. 812).

sample.recruitment: Clinic: patients who presented with lower urinary tract symptoms to the authors' service (Departments of Surgery and Pathology, St. Michael's Hospital and University of Toronto; corresponding author in the Division of Urology) (p. 810). How the patients were identified, whether they were consecutive, the period over which they were seen and how they were referred are not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated beyond chronic recreational ketamine use with genitourinary symptoms (Material and Methods, p. 810). The abstract adds that all 9 used ketamine daily and presented with severe dysuria, frequency, urgency and gross hematuria (p. 810), which the Results do not bear out for every patient (see reporting issues).
sample.demographics: Given for 3 of the 9: the index case, a 28-year-old man who smoked one pack of cigarettes a day and had a history of juvenile diabetes mellitus, hyperthyroidism and peptic ulcer disease (pp. 810–811); a 25-year-old woman; and a 17-year-old boy (p. 811). Age and sex of the other 6 are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable; no follow-up period is reported for any patient.
sample.selection_effects: Only people whose symptoms brought them to a hospital urology service are included; people who use ketamine with milder or no symptoms, or who were not referred, are absent, so the series shows the severe end of whatever range exists. How these 9 came to be reported is not stated. The authors' remark that people who use ketamine already know this as a complication rests on personal reports and is not quantified (p. 811).

exposure.measurement: The patients' own accounts in the clinical history (p. 810). No urine or blood testing for ketamine or other drugs is reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported for any patient: no amounts, duration of use or route. The abstract and the index case describe daily use (p. 810); the second patient's symptoms began soon after she started 'experimenting with ketamine' (p. 811); the remaining 6 are said to have had similar patterns of use (p. 811).
exposure.polysubstance: The authors state that none of the 9 was using other illicit drugs (Comment, p. 811), without saying how this was established. The index case smoked a pack of cigarettes a day (p. 810); alcohol and tobacco use of the others are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable at presentation. Stopping ketamine afterwards rests on the patients' accounts; how stopping was confirmed and for how long patients were followed are not reported.

comparison.controls: None: no people who use ketamine without symptoms, and no patients with other forms of ulcerative or eosinophilic cystitis examined in the same way.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Urinary history before ketamine use is reported only as the timing of onset (after daily use began in the index case; soon after first use in the second patient). The index case's diabetes and smoking are recorded but not discussed as possible contributors; for the other 8, past medical history and medicines (some medicines cause eosinophilic cystitis, p. 812) are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: History and physical examination; urine culture, urinalysis and urine cytology (and microscopy, per the abstract) in all 9; cystoscopy in all 9; bladder biopsy in 4, stained with hematoxylin-eosin, with immunohistochemistry for c-kit to identify mast cells, all read by a single pathologist; computed tomography and other tests as indicated (pp. 810–811). Computed tomography is described only for the index case (Fig. 1), as are the tests for vasculitis (p. 811). Symptoms and their course are described from the history, in words. All findings concern lasting bladder disease seen in clinic, not effects during intoxication.
outcomes.validity_norms: No symptom score, voiding diary, bladder capacity measurement or urodynamic test, and no grading of the cystoscopic or histological findings, are reported.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Ulcerative cystitis' is the cystoscopic appearance, with the histology described for the 4 biopsied; 'improvement' and 'benefit' after stopping ketamine are the authors' descriptions, without a measure or a time frame.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; the treating clinicians and the one pathologist knew the patients used ketamine.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive only; no statistics. Of 9: urine cultures sterile in all (abstract, p. 810); ulcerative cystitis at cystoscopy in all, called severe in the abstract, with the second patient's appearance described as mild squamous metaplasia with reddened flat ulcerated patches (p. 811); eosinophils in all 4 biopsies, to a variable degree (p. 812). Course after stopping ketamine: the index case's hematuria settled but disabling urgency and frequency continued; the second patient improved significantly; the third did not recover completely and was helped by pentosan polysulfate; the other 6 are said to have benefited from stopping ketamine plus pentosan polysulfate (p. 811).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a case series; no ethics approval or patient-consent statement is printed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only 3 of the 9 patients are described individually; for the other 6 there are no ages, sexes, symptoms, findings or follow-up beyond 'similar' and 'benefited' (p. 811). The abstract presents computed-tomography findings and severe ulcerative cystitis as findings of the whole series, although CT is described for one patient and one cystoscopy was mild (pp. 810–811).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Nine people with chronic recreational ketamine use at one Toronto hospital had irritative lower urinary tract symptoms, sterile urine cultures and inflamed, ulcerated bladders at cystoscopy (cytology is reported as negative for the index case; results for the others are not given); the 4 biopsies showed denuded urothelium, granulation tissue, fibrosis and eosinophils. After stopping ketamine some improved, but in two of the three patients described individually symptoms did not resolve fully; the other six are said to have benefited from stopping plus pentosan polysulfate, without any measurement.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the series describes 'severe ulcerative cystitis as a result of chronic ketamine use' and that the condition may become more prevalent (p. 810). The Comment says the temporal association between onset and cessation of use in all 9 'implicates ketamine as a causal factor', and takes one seized sample of pure ketamine hydrochloride to suggest that nothing else in recreational ketamine explains the presentation (pp. 811–812); the Conclusions call it a growing public health issue (p. 812). Nine uncontrolled cases without exposure testing or measured outcomes can raise the hypothesis but cannot show cause; the cessation half of the argument is contradicted by the index case's persisting urgency and frequency and the third patient's incomplete recovery (p. 811); one seized sample says nothing about what these patients took; and the paper contains no data on prevalence or trend.

timeline.event: This series: 9 patients in Toronto, presented by the authors as the first report of what they name ketamine-associated ulcerative cystitis (submitted June 2006).
Chu et al., BJU International: a series on destruction of the lower urinary tract in people who use ketamine (Tier A list; to be appraised from the full text).

Cottrell and Gillatt: survey of UK urologists reporting that about one-third of cases resolve after stopping ketamine, one-third stay the same and one-third may progress (as cited by Winstock et al., 2012, p. 4 of the online-first PDF; not read).
Mason et al., Clinical Radiology: radiological series on ketamine-associated lower urinary tract destruction (as cited by Winstock et al., 2012; not read).

Winstock et al.: online survey in which 26.6% of 1285 people who had used ketamine in the last year reported at least one urinary symptom they associated with ketamine; the authors describe the pathological picture (mucosal irritation, reactive atypia, eosinophilic inflammation of the lamina propria) as well recognized.
Chan et al., Hong Kong Medical Journal: systematic review and meta-analysis of ketamine-associated uropathy (Tier A list; to be appraised).

replication.where_it_stands: The clinical and pathological picture described here has since been reported by other groups (summarized by Winstock et al., 2012, pp. 1 and 4 of the online-first PDF; primary papers to be appraised), so the description is not isolated. Its causal reading, how often the condition occurs among people who use ketamine and the course after stopping rest on later work, not on this series; the systematic review of Chan et al. (2022) is to be appraised.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no funding statement or acknowledgments (pp. 810–812).
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated; the article has no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Surgery and Pathology, St. Michael's Hospital and University of Toronto; the corresponding author is in the Division of Urology (p. 810). The seized sample was obtained with the help of the Metropolitan Toronto Police Department, Narcotics Division, and analysed at an unnamed national laboratory (p. 812).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people who use ketamine regularly, with use confirmed by testing, standard urinary symptom scores, voiding diaries and bladder capacity measured at entry and repeatedly, compared with people who use other drugs but not ketamine and followed after some stop; for the pathology, biopsies graded blind against other forms of cystitis; and, for treatment, a randomized placebo-controlled trial of pentosan polysulfate in people who have stopped ketamine.

domains.note: Nine patients from one hospital service; how they were identified, over what period and whether they were consecutive is not stated; only people with symptoms severe enough to reach urology are included.
Ketamine use, its daily frequency and the absence of other illicit drugs rest on the patients' accounts; no toxicology, and no amounts, duration or route for anyone.

Cystoscopy, culture, cytology and (in 4) histology read by one pathologist are objective findings, but CT was done only as indicated, there is no symptom score, bladder-capacity measure or grading, and improvement after stopping is described in words without a follow-up period.

Infection was addressed by sterile cultures in all 9, and malignancy by cytology (reported negative for the index case only) and vasculitis by tests in the index case; but his diabetes and smoking are not discussed, medicines and allergies that cause eosinophilic cystitis are not reported as excluded for each patient, and the only contaminant check was one seized sample, not the patients' own.
Six of the 9 patients are summarized in one paragraph without age, sex, findings or follow-up; no amounts or duration of use for anyone.

domains.domain: Separation of findings from inference about cause
domains.note: Causal wording ('as a result of'; 'implicates ketamine as a causal factor') and a public-health conclusion from 9 uncontrolled cases; the association with cessation is asserted for all 9, although two of the three patients described did not fully recover.

The abstract describes all 9 as having gross hematuria and severe cystitis and reports CT findings as if for the series, while the Results describe hematuria and CT for the index case only and a mild cystoscopic appearance in the second patient (reporting issues 1 to 5).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a case series (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with the overall judgment no milder than the worst domain. The series is the first published description and may be cited for what was found in these 9 patients: the irritative symptoms, sterile urine cultures, the cystoscopic and histological appearance, and the authors' description of partial improvement after stopping ketamine, with persisting symptoms in at least two. It may not be cited for ketamine as the proven cause, for how often bladder damage occurs in people who use ketamine, for any amount or duration of use that carries risk, or for the effect of stopping ketamine or of pentosan polysulfate. A claim resting only on this series stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: Abstract: 9 patients, all described as using ketamine daily, presented with severe dysuria, frequency, urgency and gross hematuria; urine cultures were sterile in all; computed tomography showed marked thickening of the bladder wall, a small capacity and perivesicular stranding; at cystoscopy all had severe ulcerative cystitis; biopsies in 4 showed epithelial denudation and inflammation with a mild eosinophilic infiltrate; stopping ketamine, with pentosan polysulfate added, appeared to give some relief of symptoms.
key_findings.note: The Results bear out these statements only in part: hematuria and CT are described for the index case only, one cystoscopy was mild, and eosinophils predominated in the index case (reporting issues 1 to 4).

key_findings.finding: Methods: a detailed history and physical examination, cystoscopy, urine culture, urinalysis and urine cytology in all 9 patients; bladder biopsy in 4, all reviewed by a single pathologist; computed tomography and other tests as indicated.

Index case: a 28-year-old man with a 6-month history of painful hematuria, dysuria, urgency and pain after passing urine, which began only after he started using ketamine daily; he smoked one pack of cigarettes a day and had a history of juvenile diabetes mellitus, hyperthyroidism and peptic ulcer disease.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 810, right column, continuing on p. 811, left column)

key_findings.finding: Index case investigations: urine culture, urinalysis and cytology negative; computed tomography showed marked inflammatory change and a very small bladder capacity; cystoscopy showed multiple erythematous patches consistent with active cystitis; biopsy showed a substantially denuded urothelium with a thin layer of reactive and regenerating epithelial cells, an edematous superficial lamina propria with dilated vessels and scattered inflammatory cells (the appearance of granulation tissue), a dense fibrotic deeper lamina propria, and scattered lymphocytes and mast cells (c-kit immunohistochemistry) with eosinophils predominating; overall, the changes of chronic cystitis; investigations for vasculitis negative.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column); Figures 1 and 2

key_findings.finding: Index case course: antibiotic and steroid treatment did not control his symptoms; after he stopped ketamine his hematuria settled, but disabling urgency and frequency of urination continued.

Second patient: a 25-year-old woman with a 2-year history of frequency, urgency and suprapubic discomfort that began soon after she first tried ketamine; cystoscopy showed mild squamous metaplasia and reddened flat ulcerated patches; her symptoms improved significantly after she stopped ketamine. Third patient: a 17-year-old boy with recurrent dysuria and irritative voiding symptoms over several months and cystoscopic findings similar to the index case; his symptoms did not resolve completely after he stopped ketamine, other treatments had limited success, and pentosan polysulfate (Elmiron) helped relieve his irritative symptoms.

Remaining 6 patients: similar patterns of ketamine use, symptoms and cystoscopic findings; 3 had biopsies with findings similar to the index case but a variable degree of eosinophilic infiltrate; all 6 are said to have benefited from stopping ketamine with pentosan polysulfate added.
key_findings.note: No ages, sexes, durations, measurements or follow-up periods are given for these 6; stopping ketamine and pentosan polysulfate were given together, so their effects cannot be separated.

key_findings.finding: Authors' interpretation: this is the first report of the condition they name ketamine-associated ulcerative cystitis; personal reports from people who use ketamine indicate it is a well-recognized complication among them; the mechanism is unclear, possibly an active metabolite; the temporal association of onset and cessation of ketamine use with the irritative symptoms in all 9 is taken to implicate ketamine as a cause; none of the 9 was using other illicit drugs.

Seized sample: a small amount of illicit ketamine obtained with the help of the Metropolitan Toronto Police Department, Narcotics Division, was analysed at a national laboratory and found to be pure ketamine hydrochloride with only a trace of dimethyl sulfoxide; the authors take this to suggest that nothing else in recreational ketamine accounts for the presentation. They suggest that ketamine and its metabolites, which can be measured in high amounts in urine, may accumulate there and irritate the bladder.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 3rd paragraph (p. 811, right column, continuing on p. 812, left column)
key_findings.note: One sample, not from these patients; the analytical method is not reported.

key_findings.finding: Histology compared with eosinophilic cystitis: eosinophilic infiltrates were seen in all four biopsies, to a variable degree; whether they result directly from the drug or are a nonspecific inflammatory response is unclear; the authors judge the features (marked changes in the epithelium and lamina propria with granulation tissue and fibrosis) distinct from classic eosinophilic cystitis, which has been linked with bladder cancer, asthma and rhinitis, bladder outlet obstruction and medicines such as sulfonamides, warfarin and cyclophosphamide.

Conclusions: many agents tried for the irritative symptoms failed in these patients; pentosan polysulfate appeared to relieve them partially and is put forward as a possible treatment; the long-term sequelae, including fibrotic, small-capacity, noncompliant bladders, remain to be defined; management should include stopping ketamine, possibly with pentosan polysulfate.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says all 9 patients presented with severe dysuria, frequency, urgency and gross hematuria. In the Results, hematuria is described only for the index case; the second patient had frequency, urgency and suprapubic discomfort and the third dysuria and irritative voiding symptoms; the other 6 are only called similar.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's symptom list cannot be taken as describing every patient; hematuria is documented in 1 of the 3 patients described individually.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says all patients had severe ulcerative cystitis at cystoscopy; the second patient's cystoscopy showed mild squamous metaplasia with reddened flat ulcerated patches.
reporting_issues.consequence: Severity varied; 'severe' for all overstates what the Results describe.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports computed-tomography findings (marked wall thickening, small capacity, perivesicular stranding) as findings of the series; the Methods say CT was done as indicated, and the Results describe CT only for the index case (Fig. 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: How many patients had CT, and how many had these findings, is unknown; cite the CT findings for the index case only.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls the eosinophilic infiltrate mild; in the index case eosinophils predominated among the inflammatory cells, and the Comment says the degree of infiltration varied.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; eosinophil density was not graded.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes all 9 as using ketamine daily, but the second patient's symptoms began soon after she started experimenting with ketamine, and no frequency is given for the other 6 beyond similar patterns.
reporting_issues.consequence: The frequency, amount and duration of use behind these cases cannot be described from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The Comment bases the causal inference on a temporal association with both onset and cessation of ketamine use in all 9 patients, but the Results report that the index case kept disabling urgency and frequency and that the third patient's symptoms did not resolve completely after stopping.
reporting_issues.consequence: The cessation part of the argument holds only in part (the index case's hematuria; the second patient); persisting symptoms after stopping are also part of what this series shows.
